title: Plan and conduct a research project

lessons.title: Planning a workplace research project
lessons.html:
Starting with a good question

Workplace research in agriculture answers practical questions: Why are smallholders in this ward not adopting the improved maize cultivar? Does winter lick supplementation improve calving rates in the communal herd? How much water do drip-irrigated vegetables use compared with furrow irrigation? A clear, focused question is the foundation of the whole project.

Steps in planning

  1. Define the problem and why it matters to the workplace.
  2. Review existing information: departmental reports, ARC publications, extension leaflets, farm records, previous studies. Avoid repeating work already done.
  3. Write the research question and objectives. Example objective: to compare calving rates of supplemented and non-supplemented cows in two villages over one breeding season.
  4. Choose the approach: quantitative (numbers, measurements), qualitative (opinions, experiences, reasons) or both.
  5. Decide on the population and sample: who or what you will study and how you will select them, for example 30 farmers chosen randomly from the co-operative register.
  6. Select techniques for collecting data.
  7. Plan resources and time: transport, budget in ZAR, equipment, assistants, the farming calendar.
  8. Address ethics.

Research ethics

  • Get informed consent: explain the purpose and that taking part is voluntary.
  • Protect privacy and confidentiality; store personal information securely, in line with the Protection of Personal Information Act 4 of 2013.
  • Get permission from community leaders and your manager before starting.
  • Do no harm to people, animals or the environment; trials involving animal procedures need veterinary oversight.
  • Report results honestly and share them with participants.

A simple research plan

HeadingContent
Title and questionWhat you want to find out
BackgroundWhy it matters and what is known
MethodSample, techniques, analysis
TimelineActivities by month
BudgetCosts and who pays

lessons.title: Collecting and analysing data
lessons.html:
Research techniques

TechniqueGood forWatch out for
QuestionnaireMany respondents, comparable answersClear, unbiased questions; literacy and language
InterviewReasons, opinions, detailInterviewer influencing answers
Focus groupGroup views, community issuesStrong voices dominating
ObservationWhat people actually doPeople change behaviour when watched
MeasurementYields, weights, water use, soil testsCalibrated equipment, consistent method
Records and documentsPast trendsMissing or inaccurate records

Pilot-test questionnaires with three or four people before the main survey and fix confusing questions. Avoid leading questions such as Don't you agree that the new dip is better? Ask instead: How has tick control changed since the new dip was built?

Collating data

Record data on standard forms or a mobile app, number each questionnaire, enter data into a spreadsheet promptly and check entries against the originals. Keep raw data safe in case you need to recheck.

Analysing quantitative data

  • Frequencies and percentages: 18 of 30 farmers (60 percent) use certified seed.
  • Averages (mean, median) and range.
  • Comparisons between groups, for example supplemented and non-supplemented herds.
  • Cross-tabulation: adoption by age group or by gender.
  • Tables and graphs to show patterns.

Analysing qualitative data

  • Read all notes or transcripts several times.
  • Code answers into themes, such as cost, access to credit, distrust of new seed.
  • Count how often each theme comes up and pick quotes that illustrate it.

Combining both kinds of data is powerful: numbers show how many farmers do not adopt, and interviews explain why.

lessons.title: Reporting and the research environment in the workplace
lessons.html:
Writing a brief research report

  1. Title.
  2. Summary: a short paragraph with the question, method, main findings and recommendation.
  3. Introduction: the problem, background and objectives.
  4. Method: sample, techniques, period and any limitations.
  5. Findings: results with numbered tables and graphs.
  6. Discussion and conclusions: what the findings mean, compared with other information.
  7. Recommendations: practical actions for management or farmers.
  8. References and appendices: sources used, questionnaire copy.

Keep it brief and in plain language. Separate findings (what you found) from your interpretation. State limitations honestly, for example a small sample or only one season of data. Present results back to participants and the community as well as to management, in a language and format they understand.

Factors affecting research in the workplace

FactorEffect
Management supportTime, transport and funds depend on it
Budget and resourcesLimit sample size and equipment
Time pressureResearch competes with daily service delivery
SkillsStatistics and report writing may need training or a mentor
Access and trustCommunities may tire of surveys that bring no benefit
Seasons and weatherDrought or floods can disrupt field trials
Data qualityPoor farm records weaken analysis
PartnershipsUniversities and the ARC can add expertise and equipment

To improve research possibilities, link projects to organisational priorities, start small, involve farmers as co-researchers (for example on-farm trials they help design), build partnerships, and share results so the value of research becomes visible.

Key points

  • Start with a clear, focused question and measurable objectives.
  • Get informed consent, protect personal information and do no harm.
  • Pilot-test questionnaires and avoid leading questions.
  • Combine numbers with themes from interviews to explain results.
  • Report briefly and honestly, including limitations, and share results with participants.
